paragraphs.heading: A vapor in balance
paragraphs.text: Picture a liquid sealed in a closed container at a fixed temperature. Particles leave the liquid and form a vapor above its surface, and in time the escaping particles and the vapor settle into a balance, called equilibrium. The pressure that this vapor then exerts is the vapor pressure. The same idea works for a solid sitting with its own vapor.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Vapor pressure shows how strongly a liquid tends to evaporate. A substance with a high vapor pressure at ordinary temperatures is called volatile. Exact values matter in medicine for inhaled anesthetics: most of them are liquids at body temperature, yet their vapor pressure is fairly high.

paragraphs.heading: Pull between molecules
paragraphs.text: Liquids whose molecules attract each other strongly tend to have low vapor pressures, and weak attraction gives high ones. Warming a liquid makes that attraction count for less against the draw of the gas phase, so the vapor pressure goes up. The rise is not a straight line, and it is often described by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation.

paragraphs.heading: What boiling really is
paragraphs.text: A liquid's normal boiling point is the temperature at which its vapor pressure equals the pressure of the air around it, defined as 1 atmosphere, 760 Torr or 101.325 kPa. Warm it a little past that point and the vapor can overcome the atmosphere, so bubbles of vapor form inside the liquid. Deeper in the liquid, bubbles need a slightly higher temperature, because the weight of fluid above adds pressure.

paragraphs.heading: An example: methyl chloride
paragraphs.text: As a general rule, liquids with lower boiling points have higher vapor pressures at room temperature. Methyl chloride shows this clearly on a chart comparing several liquids. At every temperature shown, its vapor pressure is the highest of the group. Its normal boiling point, −24.2 °C, is also the lowest of them.

paragraphs.heading: How it is measured
paragraphs.text: Vapor pressure is given in ordinary pressure units. The SI unit is the pascal, one newton per square meter, while medicine sometimes uses millimeters of mercury. Measuring it is simple for common pressures between 1 and 200 kPa. You purify the substance, seal it in a container, remove any foreign gas, and read the pressure of its vapor at different temperatures. Readings below 1 kPa carry large errors.
